*103.   SHRI THANGA TAMIL SELVAN:† 
 PROF. SAIF-UD-DIN SOZ: 
Will the Minister of HOME AFFAIRS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that incidents of rape including minors is on the 
rise in the country; 
(b) the steps taken by Government to prevent this heinous crime; and 
(c) whether Government would consider imposing death penalty on rapist 
by amending the existing criminal law? 
THE MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS (SHRI SHIVRAJ V PATIL): (a) to 
(c) A Statement is laid on the Table of the House. 
Statement 
(a) As per statistics complied by the National Crimes Record Bureau, 
the number of incidents of rape reported in the years 2001,2002 and 2003 
were 16075,16373 and 15847 respectively. Out of these, the number of 
incidents of rape of minors during the same period were 2113,2532 and 
 †The question was actually asked on the floor of the house by Shri Thanga Tamil Selvan. 
16 

[9 March, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
2949 respectively. Total number of incidents of rape cases in 2004 (upto 
September-provisional) is 12414. 
(b) 'Public Order' and 'Police' are State subjects as per the Seventh 
Schedule to the constitution of India and, as such, registration, investigation, 
detection and prevention of crime is primarily the responsibility of the State 
Governments. However, the Government of India has been issuing advisories 
to the State Governments from time to time to make concerted efforts to 
improve the administration of Criminal Justice System and to take effective 
measures to control crimes against vulnerable sections including women 
and children. In an advisory sent to the State Governments in May, 2004, 
the following points have been re-emphasized: 
i. There should be no delay in registration of FIR in cases of Crime 
Against Women. 
ii. Cases should be thoroughly investigated and charge-sheets filed 
within three months from the date of occurrence of crime, 
iii. Women Police Cells be set up in all police stations. Exclusive 
women police stations may also be set up to cater especially to 
women, 
iv. Police officials charged with the responsibility of protecting women 
should be sensitized adequately, 
v. Women police officials in the State Police Force should be 
recruited widely, 
vi. Institutional support should be provided to victims of violence, 
and 
vii. There should be proper counseling to victims of rape. 
(c) The existing provisions of the Indian Penal Code, 1860, prescribe a 
sentence upto life imprisonment in case of offence of rape. The Law 
Commission and the Committee constituted for making recommendations 
for Criminal Justice System have not recommended death penalty for the 
offence of rape. There is no proposal under Government's consideration to 
introduce the sentence of death penalty for those guilty of rape. 
SHRI THANGA TAMIL SELVAN: Sir, as started by the hon. Minister, 
the number of incidents of rape of minors has increased from 2113 in 2001 
to 2949 in 2003. These figures indi cate only the reported cases. Hon. 
Minister, these figures indicate only the reported cases, and because of 
our social system, many cases of rape go unreported. So, I would like to 
17

know from the hon. Minister, what are the reasons for the increasing incidents 
of rape as assessed by the Government, 
SHRI SHIVRAJ V. PAUL: Sir, there are many reasons and they are 
known to the hon. Member also...(Interruption)....Now, there are all kinds 
of posters by the sides of the road, there are all kinds of literature, all 
kinds of scenes and there is the liberal attitude which is adopted by the 
humanity now. There are many other things also. I would not blame only 
the individuals. The system may also be suffering from some defects. 
There are many other reasons. And I agree with you that these are only 
the reported cases. There may be some unreported cases also. Now, 
under the circumstances, the Governm ent is doing what it can and it 
would like to do more than what it is doing now if some more information is 
given. But the kind of society in which we live, the kind of psychology that 
is developing, the kind of material which becoming available to all of us 
and the kind of attitude we are adopting towards life, in my opinion, are all 
responsible for this. 
SHRI THANGA TAMIL SELVAN: It is clear that existing laws are not 
adequate to curb this heinous crime. It is seen that in countries, where 
capital punishment is awarded, incidents of rape are rare. Therefore, will 
the hon. Minister consider imposing death penalty for rapists? 
SHRI SHIVRAJ V. PATIL: Sir, we are having a Bill before us. At present, 
it is in Rajya Sabha and it is moved in the House in order to amend the 
Criminal Procedure Code and the Indian Penal Code. There are other steps 
which we are going to take up to see that this kind of crime is not there. 
But, whether to provide death punishment for rape or not, is a question 
which is not acceptable to many in the society, while some are suggesting 
that this kind of punishment should be provided. Whether providing this 
kind of sentence, that is, death sentence, will reduce the number of crimes 
taking place, is also a doubtful proposition. Sometimes, they say when 
death sentence is provided, the victim is likely to be killed also. Sometimes, 
they say that when death sentence is provided, the law is used in such a 
fashion and the rules, that are m ade, and Supreme Court judgements, 
which are given, that in the rarest of the rare cases, death punishment 
should be given. Now, because all those things, providing death sentence 
in the Indian Penal Code, in the opinion of many, is not going to help in 
seeing that the rape incidents are reduced. So, that is the problem which 
has to be decided by all of us who are sitting in the Legislature. Now, on 
this question, I think, today, they are saying that death sentence should 
be abolished. Many of the countries have abolished death sentence, and

have to understand is that for anything, which is happening in the country,

stands, there are areas given to the States Governments to be dealt with

Additional Grants to Naxal Affected States 
 
*104. SHRIMATI HEMA MALINI: Will the Minister of HOME AFFAIRS 
be pleasd to state: 
(a) whether Union Government propose to float a plan providing additional 
grants to naxal hit States for road construction to contain insurgecy in the 
country; 
(b) if so, the details thereof; and 
(c) the existing present grant allocated to backward districts affected 
by Naxalism? 
THE MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS (SHRI SHIVRAJ V. PATH): (a) to 
(c) A statement is laid on the Table of the House. 
Statement 
(a) to (c) The Backward District Initiative (BDI) component of the Rashtriya 
Sam Vikas Yojana (RSVY) also covers 55 naxal affected districts in 9 
States. This scheme provides an additionality of Rs. 15 crores as special 
Central assistance on 100% grant basis per year per district for a period of 
3 years so as to fill in critical gaps in social and physical infrastructure in 
these districts including for construction of roads. Road construction in 
naxal affected areas can also be taken up under the Pradhan Mantri Gram 
Sadak Yojana (PMGSY). However, there is no specific plan/proposal to 
provide funds to naxal affected States for road construction to deal with 
naxalism. 
SHRIMATI HEMA MALINI: I would like to know from the hon. Minister 
whether the Government intends to make a unified command for all the 
States and the Centre to fight this menace jointly. What are the rehabilitation 
plans made for surrendered naxalites? 
SHRI SHIVRAJ V. PATH: Sir, we have taken steps in consultation with 
the State Governments. Whatever the State Governments are suggesting 
and whatever can be accepted by the Union Government, we have accepted. 
We have not waited for the State Governments to make suggestions; we 
have ourselves given them help in many, many cases. What we are d is 
this. We are giving them paramilitary forces to deal with naxalite activities in 
the States. Up to this time, we were charging some money for the 
paramilitary forces supplied to them. We have taken a decision recently 
not to charge a single pie from the State Governments for this purpose. 
We are giving some funds to the State Governments to see that the areas,

which are not developed, and areas, which are infested with naxalite 
activities, are developed. We call it the Backward Area Development Fund, 
and this fund is used to create infrastructure and to help the people to get 
employment and many other things. We are giving funds to the State 
Governments to meet the expenditure they incur in dealing with naxalite 
activities. Now, we are asking them to increase the number of persons 
and officers in their forces to deal with these kind of things and other law

enormous. Sometimes the money, which is given, is not spent. I am not 
blaming anybody, maybe they have some other difficulties also, but we 
are helping in this fashion. So, we are jointly trying to deal with this situation. 
But as the constitutional and the legal provisions prevail, we shall have to 
understand that this has to be done through the State Governments and 
we are trying to do all that is necessary and possible for this.

Potential of wind energy to meet power deficit 
*112. SHRI GIREESH KUMAR SANGHI: 
DR. T. SUBBARAMI REDDY: 
Will the Minister of NON-CONVENTIONAL ENERGY SOURCES be 
pleased to state: 
(a) whether expanding at rate of over 30 percent per annum, the 
wind energy sector in India promises to emerge as an economically viable 
option to meet current power deficit of the country; 
(b) whether with 100's of wind turbines producing clean green energy at 
an economically competitive cost, t he/Indian wind energy market is 
emerging as the third most rapidly growing wind market in the world after 
German and Spain; and 
(c) if so, what are steps Government propose to take to improve wind 
energy further in the country to meet power shortage? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE OF THE MINISTRY OF NON-
CONVENTIONAL ENERGY SOURCES (SHRI VILAS MUTTEMWAR): (a) 
Grid interactive Wind Power installed capacity has progressively increased 
from about 250 MW in 2002-03 to about 500 MW in 2004-05 (April-
December, 2004) with an average annual growth rate of about 25%. A 
cumulative installed capacity of 2980 MW has been achieved as on 
31.12.2004 in the country. Wind powe r requires a set of incentives to 
remain competitive, including prefer ential tariff. Considering that the 
potential for setting up wind power projects exists only in 10 States, the 
intermittent nature of such power supply and its low capacity utilization 
factor, wind power is expected to play a supplemental role. However, the 
aim is that 5% of additional grid interactive power installed capacity would 
come from wind energy during the 10th and 11th plan periods. 
(b) The Country currently ranks at fifth position in the world after Germany, 
USA, Spain and Denmark in the wind power installed capacity. During the 
first two years of the Tenth Plan, 10% of the additional grid interactive 
power installed capacity has come from wind energy. 
(c) Wind power progress in the country till date is highly satisfactorily. 
Apart from preferential tariff in most potential States, few major components 
of wind electric turbine systems attract a concenssional rate of custom 
35 

RAJYA SABHA [9 March, 2005] 
duty of only 5%. In addition, 80% of the accelerated depreciation is available 
to wind power companies. Wind electric generator manufacturer is exempt 
from payment of central excise du ty. Resource assessment and R&D 
support is being provided by Centre for Wind Energy Technology, an 
institution under the administrative control of this Ministry.

Indo-Pak economic cooperation 
(c) and (d) The First Meeting of this JSG was held at New Delhi on 22-

THE MINISTER OF COMMERCE AND INDUSTRY (SHRI KAMAL 
NATH): (a) Yes, Sir. 
(b) The fall in prices of tea during the last few years, coupled with high 
costs of production, sluggish rate  of growth in domestic demand and 
increased age of tea bushes have adversely affected the viability of tea 
gardens, particularly the medium sized and financially weak, resulting in 
closure/abandonment of some tea gardens in the country. This has caused 
problems of unemployment for workers in these tea gardens. 
(c) and (d) The Plantations Labour Act, 1951 provides for the welfare of 
plantation labour and regulates the co nditions of work in Plantations, 
including tea. This Act is administered by the State Governments, who are 
the appropriate authorities under the said Act to monitor the implementation 
of the various provisions in the Act. The Act also empowers the State 
Governments to make appropriate rules in this regard. Tea Board also 
supports some welfare programmes and activities for the benefit of tea 
plantation workers and their dependants in education and health care 
through their regular plan schemes. Several measures have been taken 
by the Government to assist the tea industry to tide over the situation. 
These include implementation of a Special Tea Term Loan envisaging 
restructuring/rephasing of irregular portion of outstanding term/working 
capital loans in the tea sector with repayment over 5 to 7 years with a 
moratorium of 1 year, implementation of a price subsidy scheme for small 
tea growers, introduction of a Price sharing formula for ensuring fair return

improving the quality of tea and thereby improving the prices etc. In addition,

Statement 
Objectives, constitution and functions of national manufacturing 
competitiveness council 
OBJECTIVES 
The Main objective of NMCC is to provide a continuing forum for policy 
dialogue to energize and sustain the growth of manufacturing sectors which 
have potential for global competitiveness, current strengths and constraints 
of identified sectors, and recommend National level industry/sector specific 
policy initiatives as may be required for augmenting the growth of 
manufacturing sector. 
50 

[9 March, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
COMPOSITION 
Composition of the National Manufacturing Competitiveness Council 
consists of Chairman in the rank of Cabinet Minister. 24 Members to the 
Commission from various fields including senior Government functionaries, 
Professionals, representatives from Apex Industrial Organizations and 
various industrial sectors have been appointed vide Notification dated 
25th November, 2004, besides Member Secretary in the rank of Secretary 
to the Government of India. 
FUNCTIONS 
The National Manufacturing Competitiveness Council (NMCC) will advise 
the Government on industrial and sector specific initiatives that may be 
required for enhancing competitiveness of industries which would include 
sectoral and enterprise level init iatives, innovation and technology 
development (R&D), entrepreneurship promotion, infrastructure and enabling 
facilities, trade and fiscal policies and employment generation.

SHRI ABU ASIM AZMI:

71 

RAJYA SABHA [9 March, 2005] 
(b) if so, the details thereof and action taken against the officers

(c) whether it is also a fact that Indian Navy incurred a loss of several 
lakhs of rupees on account of procurement of substandard equipments for 
air conditioning plant in the logistic department; and 
(d) if so, what action has been taken against the officials concerned? 
THE MINISTER OF DEFENCE (SHRI PRANAB MUKHERJEE): (a) to 
(d) It is a fact that during 1993—1995, the Naval Headquarters had authorized 
Material Organisation Visakhapatnam to procure spares through Indian 
trade (ship chandler purchase). 
A majority of the ships and submarines based at Visakhapatnam, 
acquired between 1967—1991, were of Soviet Union origin. With the 
disintegration of the Soviet Union (in August 1991), there was a breakdown 
in the supply of spares and components for these Soviet origin Naval 
Platforms. This was due to the non availability of information about the 
Original Equipment Manufacturers (OEM) in the erstwhile Soviet Union. 
Before the disintegration of the Soviet Union, the Navy's requirements 
of spares and components were being routed through two Soviet 
Government channelising agencies i.e., General Engineering Department 
(GED) and General Technical Department (GTD). The Indian Navy did not 
have a sufficient data base about the market prices of Soviet supplies, as 
before 1991 these were supplied on Friendship Prices', by GET/GTD. 
Allegations of malpractices against ship chandler purchase were received 
by Naval Headquarters. These allegations were examined by the Central 
Vigilance Commission (CVC) and also investigated by the CBI. However, 
no malafide in such purchases was established and the case was closed 
by the CBI. 
During November 1995 an Indian Naval Ship had reported failure of air 
conditioning equipment whilst at sea. A Board of Inquiry was thereafter 
convened to investigate the allegation of procurement of substandard AC 
chillers. The Board of Inquiry did not establish any nexus and consequent 
malafide intent on part of the concerned individuals.

NHRC guidelines for arrests 
823. SHRI JANARDHANA POOJARY: W ill the Minister of HOME 
AFFAIRS be pleased to state:

comprehensive guidelines on the arrest of a person; and

THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HOME AFFAIRS 
(SHRI SRIPRAKASH JAISWAL): (a) and (b) The National Human Rights 
Commission (NHRC) has issued comprehensive guidelines on the arrest 
of a person and circulated these to all the police stations in the country for 
effective implementation. The guidelines provide, inter alia, that in case of 
arrest, the authorities concerned should exercise proper restraint and make 
the arrest only after being fully satisfied of the genuineness of their action, 
power of arrest is justified in cognizable cases only for those involved in 
heinous offences or are prone to violent behaviour and likely to commit 
further offences or where the susp ect requires to be prevented from

force and upholding the dignity of the person while making arrest, avoiding 
the use of handcuffs or leg chains except as provided under the law, 
association of women police officers as far as practicable where the person 
or persons arrested are women, avoidance of arrest of women between 
sunset and sunrise etc. The guidelines also refer to the requirements to 
be followed for effecting arrests as laid down in the orders of the Supreme 
Court in the Joginder Kumar's case-(1994) 4SCC 260 and D.K. Basu's 
case (1997)1 SCC. 
The Government has also advised all the State Governments/Union 
Territories to follow all the requirements laid down by the Hon'ble Supreme 
Court in the case of D.K. Basu Vs. State of West Bengal whenever arrests 
are made.

for distinguished service, in any field. All recommendations received for

into the system of granting awards , review the existing guidelines and 
suggest criteria for selection of persons for padma Awards. The 
recommendations of the Committee were accepted by the Government 
and have been implemented. 
The normal practice is to informally seek the consent of the persons 
selected for the awards before the awards are announced. However, due 
to paucity of time, non-availability of some such persons at the known

867. SHRI K. RAMA MOHANA RAO:  Will the Minister of NON-
CONVENTIONAL ENERGY SOURCES be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is true that Gove rnment are preparing a National 
Hydrogen Road Map and also thinking of launching a national mission 
on bio-diesel as a part of its efforts to encourage the use of alternative 
fuels; 
(b) whether it is also true that Government have also identified the 
Ministry of Rural Development as the nodal Ministry for this purpose; 
and 
(c) how the National Hydrogen Energy Board provide guidelines for 
making and implementing hydrogen energy? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE OF THE MINISTRY OF NON-
CONVENTIONAL ENERGY SOURCES (SHRI VILAS MUTTEMWAR): 
(a) Ministry of Non-Conventional Energy Sources have constituted a 
National Hydrogen Energy Board under which a Steering Group has 
been set up to prepare a National Hydrogen Road Map. The Planning 
Commission's Report—2003 on Development of Bio-fuel has 
recommended launching of a National Mission on Bio-diesel as part of 
the efforts to encourage use of alternative fuels.

(b) The Ministry of Rural Development has been made the Nodal Ministry 
for processing the recommendations of the Report of the Planning 
Commission on Development of Bio-fuel. 
(c) National Hydrogen Energy Board consisting of Secretaries of various 
concerned Ministries, high level repr esentatives of industry and their 
associations, academia and other exper ts reviews different aspects of 
hydrogen energy including its production, storage, transportation, delivery 
and applications for transportation and power generation through a 
consultative process with the objective of providing guidelines in the 
preparation and implementation of the National Hydrogen Energy Road 
Map.

Wind energy for meeting power deficit 
869.   SHRI B.J. PANDA: 
SHRI KRIPAL PARMAR: 
Will the Minister of NON-CONVENTIONAL ENERGY SOURCES be 
pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that the wind energy sector in our country is 
emerging as an economically viable option to meet the current power 
deficit in different States; 
(b) whether renowned industrialists and other eminent personalities 
have been investing in this sector to exploit the potential; 
(c) whether the installed capacity in this sector is increasing at a fast 
pace and that the nation could be one of the biggest wind power producers 
in the world; and 
(d) if so, action-plan of the Government to harness the gains of this 
pollution-free source of energy? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE OF THE MINISTRY OF NON-
CONVENTIONAL ENERGY SOURCES (SHRI VILAS MUTTEMWAR): 
(a) A cumulative installed capacity of around 3000 MW. has been 
achieved as on 31.12.2004 in the country. Wind power requires a set of 
incentives to remain competit ive including preferential tariff. 
Considering that the potential for setting up wind power projects exists 
only in 10 States, the intermittent nature of such power supply and its 
low capacity utilization factor, wi nd power is expected to play a 
supplemental role. However, the aim is that 5% of additional grid interactive 
power installed capacity would come from wind energy during the 10th 
and 11th plan period. 
(b) Yes, Sir. 
(c) Yes, Sir. The installed capacity of wind power projects has increased 
from 242 MW in 2002-03 to 615 MW in 2003-04 and it is expected to 
increase in 2004-05. India presently ranks at the fifth position in the 
world in terms of wind power installed capacity. 
(d) Grid Interactive Wind Power Programme is essentially private sector 
driven. The steps taken by the Government to promote setting up of 
wind power projects include concessional import duty for wind electricity 
131 

RAJYA SABHA [9 March, 2005] 
generator sub-systems, excise duty exemption, ten years tax holiday on 
power projects, benefit of accelerated depreciation and loan from Indian 
Renewable Energy Development Agency (IREDA) and other financial 
institutions. Wind resource assessment studies are supported in various States 
for identifying new areas for deployment of wind power projects. Wind power is 
being given preferential tariffs in respective States. 
Private participation in power sector 
870. DR. MAM. RAMASWAMY: Will the Minister of POWER be 
pleased to state: 
(a) the steps taken by the Centra l Government to improve private 
participation in power sector; 
(b) whether there has been certain road-blocks which are hindering private 
participation in power sector; 
(c) if so, the details thereof; and 
(d) the steps taken by Central Government to remove these road-blocks? 
THE MINISTER OF POWER (SHRI P.M. SAYEED): (a) The 
Electricity Act, 2003 which has come into effect from 10th June, 2003 
contains several measures to attrac t private investment in the power 
sector. Government has also initiated the process of reforms and re-
structuring of power sector which would improve the finances of the 
power utilities thereby attracting private investments. 
Under the Act, thermal generation has been fully delicensed and 
captive generation has been freely permitted, Central and State 
Regulatory Commissions have been set up and power trading has 
been recognized as an independent activity. 
Under the provisions of the Act, open access in transmission has 
been introduced to promote competition amongst the generating 
companies who can now sell to diferent distribution licensees across 
the country. Guidelines for competitive bidding for procurement of 
power by distribution licensees under the Electricity Act, 2003 have 
been issued.. 
The National Common Minimum Programme has reiterated the 
commitment of the Government to an increased role for private 
generation of power and more importan tly, in power distribution. From 
time to time, Government has taken serveral measures to increase 
private investment 
132 

[9 March, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
in the power sector. Also, 100% Foreign Direct Investment has been 
permitted in projects for elec tricity generation, transmission and 
distribution. 
(b) and (c) The major road-blocks which are hindering private participation in 
power sector are as follows: 
(i) Inability of SEBs and State Governments to provide an acceptable 
payment security. The revenues of the SEBs are not adequate, to ensure 
payments to Independent Power Producers. This is due to skewed tariffs and 
poor collection efficiencies. 
(ii) Delay in finalisation of various contracts such as PPA, Fuel Supply 
Agreement and Fuel Transportation Agreement acceptable to all the 
concerned parties. Protracted negotia tions on fuel prices, liquidated 
charges/damages, risk covering clauses etc. have caused delays in 
achieving financial closure in many cases. 
(iii) Court cases in the form of Public Interest Petitions etc. 
(iv) Withdrawal by equity holders and EPC contractors. 
(d) The initiatives taken by the Government as mentioned in reply to part (a), 
particularly regarding the reform and restructuring of power sector including SEB's, 
formulation of Central & State Regulatory Commissions, recognizing power 
trading as an independent activity etc. are expected to boost the confidence of the 
investors. Government has also been assisting to resolve issues coming in the 
way of the private sector power projects achieving financial closure. An Inter-
Institutional Group (IIG) comprising senior representatives from the financial 
institutions as well as from the Ministry of Power, has been instrumental in 
facilitiating financial closure of 11 private power projects having a total capacity of 
over 4000 MW in the last one year.

Tariff Structure in Power Sector 
888. SHRI SANJAY NIRUPAM: Will the Minister of POWER be pleased 
to state : 
(a) whether Government have revised the tariff in Power Sector; 
(b) whether the recovery of capital costs in the power tariff would be 
front loaded or back loaded; 
(c) the details about the tariff structure and its sudden impact upon the 
Power Sector; and 
(d) whether common people are the ultimate bearer for the above ? 
THE MINISTER OF POWER (SHRI P.M. SAYEED):(a) to (d) Under 
the Electricity Act, 2003, the tariff for supply of power to various 
categories of consumers is to be determined by the State Electricity 
151 

RAJYA SABHA [9 March, 2005] 
Regulatory Commissions (SERCs) and in doing so these Commissions are 
required to be guided by the provisions contained in Section 61 of the Act 
which, inter alia, include the factors which would encourage competition, 
efficiency, economical use of the resources, safeguarding of consumer's 
interest and at the same time ensure recovery of the cost of electricity in a 
reasonable manner. The State Commissions are also required to ensure 
transparency while exercising its powers and discharging its functions. 
The SERCs shall also be guided by the principles and methodologies specified 
by the Central Commission for determination of the tariff applicable to generating 
companies and transmission licensees. 
In the terms and conditions of tariff for the peirod 1.4.2004 to 
31.03.2009, Central Electricity Regulatory Commission has provided that 
depreciation would be permitted applying straight line method spread over 
the life of the asset. In addition, advance against depreciation shall also allowed 
to meet debt services obligations by considering the repayment period of 
loan as 10 years. The fixed cost goes on reducing as the assets gets 
depreciated. 
Section 63 of the Electricity Act, 2003 provides that the Appropriate 
Commission shall adopt the tariff if such tariff has been determined through 
transparent process of bidding in accordance with the guidelines issued by the 
Central Government. 
Central Government has issued the guidelines for competitive bidding for 
determination of tariff for procurement of power by distribution licensees. These 
guidelines, inter-alia, provide flexibility to bidders by laying down that ratio of 
minimum and maximum capacity charge for any year shall not be less than 0.7 
to avoid excessive front loading or back loading during the period of contract.

Target for export of textiles 
914. SHRI NAND KISHORE YADAV: Will the Minister of TEXTILES be 
pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government have fixed any target for export of textile by 
2010; 
 
(b) if so, the details thereof; 
(c) whether it is also a fact that India has missed the opportunities of 
new capacities earlier during quota regime; 
(d) if so, the reasons therefor; and 
(e) the steps taken by Government to meet the challenges in the sector 
from other countries? 
THE MINISTER OF TEXTILES (SHRI SHANKERSINH VAGHELA): (a) 
and (b) The New Textile Policy (NTxP-2000) makes a vision statement to 
achieve textile and apparel exports of US$ 50 billion by 2010. However, 
the textile export targets are fixed on year to year basis, keeping in view 
the most recent export trends and potential for future growth in different 
textile sub-sectors. For the year 200 4-05, the textile export target has 
been fixed at US$ 15.2 billion. 
(c) and (d) India's textile exports to the major importing countries (United 
States, European Union, Canada) had been circumscribed by the annual 
quota limits placed by these countries under the erstwhile quota regime, 
which has had an adverse impact of flow of investments in India's textile 
sector. As the date for the final integr ation of quota restrictions started 
approaching, encouraged with the Government's initiatives, the industry 
has taken definitive steps by making consideralle investments to restructure 
the industry through modernisation and expansion of capacities. 
(e) Government has been taking a number of steps from time to time to 
strengthen the Indian textile indust ry to meet the emerging global 
competition. Some of the important initiatives taken are: 
(i) The Technology Upgradation Fund Scheme (TUFS) has been made 
operational from 1 -4-1999 to facilitate the modernisation and upgradation 
of the sector. 
181 

RAJYA SABHA [9 March, 2005] 
(ii) The imports of specified textiles and garment machinery items has 
been allowed at concessional rate of customs duty to encourage 
investments and to make our textile products competitive in the global 
market. The cost of machinery has also been reduced through fiscal policy 
measures. 
(iii) To improve the productivity and quality of cotton, Government has 
launched Technology Mission on Cotton (TMC). The mission comprises 
four mini-missions, which are being jointly implemented by the Ministry of 
Agriculture and Ministry of Textiles. One of the important ingredients of 
the Mission is to cotton processing facilities by upgrading/modernizing 
the existing ginning and pressing facilities and setting up of new market 
yards/improvement of existing market yards. 
(iv) The Government has launched a centrally sponsored scheme titled 
"Apparel Park for Export Scheme" for imparting focused thrust for setting 
up of apparel manufacturing units of international standards at potential 
growth centres to give fillip to exports. 
(v) For upgrading infrastructure facilities at important textile centres, a 
scheme titled 'Textile Centre Infrastructure Development Scheme" (TCIDS) 
has been launched. 
(vi) The fiscal duty structure has been generally rationalised to achieve 
growth and maximum value addition. Except for mandatory excise duty 
on polyester filament yarn, synthetic and artificial fibres and synthetic and 
artificial filament yarns, the whole value addition chain including cotton 
textile and cotton clothing items have been given excise exemption option. 
Additional Excise Duty on Textiles & Textile Articles (AT&T) and Additional 
Excise Duty (Goods of Special Importance) Act have been abolished. 
(vii) The Government has de-reserved the woven segment of readymade 
garment from the SSI sector. It has also raised the SSI investment limit for 
knitted segment to Rs. 5 crores. In the Union Budget 2005-06, an 
announcement has been made for de-reservation of 30 hosiery items from 
the SSI. 
(viii) National Institute for Fashion Technology (NIFT), its six branches 
and Apparel Training & Design Centres (ATDCs) are running various 
courses/programmes to meet skilled manpower requirements of textile 
industry especially apparel in t he field of design, merchandising and 
marketing. 
182

State languages in school curriculum 
*82. SHRI SANJAY RAUT: Will the Minister of HUMAN RESOURCE 
DEVELOPMENT be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that some of the State Governments have made 
their State language compulsory in the primary and secondary level school 
curriculum; 
(b) if so, the details thereof; 
(c) what would be the impact of su ch decision if other States also 
follow; 
(d) whether Government have taken any decision in the matter to make 
State language compulsory in primary and secondary level school's 
curriculum; and 
(e) if so, the details thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF HUMAN R ESOURCE DEVELOPMENT (SHRI 
ARJUN SINGH): (a) to (c) The Government is not aware whether any 
State Governments have made their respective State languages 
compulsory in the primary and secondary school curriculum. At the national 
level, the National Council of Educational Research and Training (NCERT) 
prepares the curriculum for school education. The Central Board of 
191 

RAJYA SABHA [9 March, 2005] 
Secondary Education (CBSE) adopts/adapts this curriculum for its affiliated 
schools only. The State Education Bo ards are not bound to follow the 
curriculum prepared by the NCERT. They are empowered to prepare their 
own curriculum for their respective schools. The subject "Education" being 
on the Concurrent List, information re lating to the actions by the State 
Governments about making State language compulsory in their respective 
curricula is not centrally available. However, as per Article 350A, it is the 
responsibility of the State and of every local authority within the State to 
provide adequate facilities for instruct ions in the mother-tongue at the 
primary stage. 
The Three Language Formula as advocated in the National Policy on 
Education was approved by the Parliament. The formula is applicable at 
the upper primary stage and has to continue upto the end of Secondary 
stage i.e. Class X. This formula provides for a study of the mother tongue 
or the regional language compulsorily as the first language. It also requires 
the study of Hindi, English and a modern Indian language, preferably one 
of the Southern languages in the Hindi speaking, Hindi and English in the 
non-Hindi speaking States. The National Curriculum Framework for School 
Education (NCFSE) 2000 of the NCERT has also included the provisions 
of the Three Language Formula. 
This formula, which flows from a policy decision, is to be reflected in 
the school curriculum. The role of the Central Government in the matter of 
the implementation of the formula is recommendatory. The implementation 
of the Three Language Formula is the sole responsibility of the State 
Governments. All the States/Union Territories had, accordingly, been urged 
by the Government from time to time to implement it. While all the schools 
affiliated to the Central Board of Secondary Education (CBSE) and the 
Council for the Indian School Certificate Examination (CISCE) have already 
implemented it, most of the States/UTs, too, are implementing this formula. 
(d) No, Sir. 
(e) Does not arise.

Closure of Private Universities 
*84.    SHRI MANOJ BHATTACHARYA:  
 SHRI AMAR SINGH: 
Will the Minister of HUMAN RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT be 
pleased to state: 
(a) whether about a hundred private universities in different parts of 
the country have been closed following  a recent judgement of the 
Supreme Court of India; 
(b) if so, the details thereof; and 
(c) the steps proposed to be taken by Government to protect interest 
of a large number of affected students? 
THE MINISTER OF HUMAN RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT (SHRI 
ARJUN SINGH): (a) and (b) The Supreme Court of India vide its 
judgment dated 11 February, 2005 in writ Petition (Civil) No. 19/2004: 
Prof. Yash Pal & Ors. Vs. State of Chhattisgarh & Ors., has declared 
the provisions of Section 5 and 6,  of the Chhattisgarh Niji Kshetra 
Vishwavidyalaya (SthapanaAur Viniyaman) Adhiniyam, 2002, to be 
ultra vires of the Constitution. All notifications issued by the State 
Government in the Gazette in the purported exercise of powers under 
Section 5 of the aforesaid Act, notifying the Universities, have been 
quashed and such Universities cease to exist. The Supreme Court also 
held that "the impugned Act which specifically makes a provision enabling 
a University to have an off-campus center outside the State is deary 
beyond the legislative competence of  the Chhattisgarh legislature." 
The Supreme Court also directed that if any institutions have been 
established by such Universities, steps may be taken for their affiliation to 
already existing State Universities. 
(c) In view of above, the Chhattisgarh Government has been 
requested to inform whether any specific intervention is required to be 
taken by the Government of India in the matter. The UGC has also 
been requested to examine the judgement and its implications, 
particularly for the bonafide students en rolled with these "universities' 
so that, should the need arise, the Commission could be requested to 
take appropriate steps in the matter.

(i) Sand flushing into active fire zone from surface to under ground 
through boreholes. 
(ii) Surface blanketing to prevent breathing in of air to the fire area. 
(iii) Inert gas flushing from surface through boreholes to extinguish 
fire. 
(iv) Quenching of spot fire and mining out the quenched coal. 
(v) Sealing of the part of the mine under fire by construction of the fire 
stoppings/isolation stoppings. 
(vi) Application of fire resistant sealant in and around the isolation 
stoppings/fire stoppings. 
(vii) Regular monitoring with the help of Co-detectors, toximeter, air 
sampling and analysis of the same at colliery level. 
(viii) Trench cutting by mechanized means to excavate fire and to 
prevent spread of the same.

646.   SHRI R.P. GOENKA: 
PROF. R.B.S. VARMA: 
Will the Minister of HUMAN RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT be pleased 
to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that a proposal has been formulated to introduce 
the study of disaster management in the school curriculum so as to prepare 
and equip the students, teachers and the management to handle any 
crisis in the school or outside; and

to co-ordinate with the State Governments to finalise the contents of the 
theoretical course (s) and practical training to adequately equip the 
with life skills, and for speedy implementation of the proposal?

DEVELOPMENT (SHRI M.A.A. FATMI): (a) and (b) The National Curriculum 
Framework for School Education is presently under review. The National 
Council of Educational Research and Training (NCERT) has set up a 
National Steering Committee under the Chairmanship of Prof. Yash Pal to 
undertake the review. In addition, 21 National Focus Groups have also 
been set up to produce research based position papers in the major areas 
of the curriculum. The National focus Group on Health and Physical 
Education includes safety items. The Focus Groups on Habitat and

Mushrooming of Private Technical Institutes 
649. SHRI B.J. PANDA: Will the Minister of HUMAN RESOURCE 
DEVELOPMENT be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that Government have expressed concern on the 
mushrooming of private technical institutes in the country; 
(b) whether Government are aware that these private technical institute 
can create problems for the students co ming out of these institutes in 
getting job; and 
247 

RAJYA SABHA [9 March, 2005] 
(c) if so, what is Government's reaction to regularise these institutes 
inorder to address grievances of the students of these institutes? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HUMAN RESOURCE 
DEVELOPMENT (SHRI M.A.A. FATMI): (a) to (c) The Government has 
permitted private initiative in technical edcuation since there is demand for 
technical manpower within the country as well as in the global market. 
The All India Council for Technical Education (AICTE) has been mandated 
to assure quality in technical education. The Council has laid down strict 
norms and standards for setting up new institutions of technical education 
and for introduction of new technical courses in existing institutions. The 
expansion in technical education is necessary, especially in the emerging 
areas of technology so as to keep pace with the global as well as national 
demand for technical manpower. The AICTE ensures that the quality of 
these institutions is constantly  monitored and upgraded so that the 
manpower produced by these colleges is accepted globally as well as 
nationally. For awareness of students, a list of approved technical institutes 
has been made available on the website of AICTE (www.aicteernet.in). 
AICTE also publishes notices, from time to time, in leading newspapers, 
cautioning all concerned to check t he approval status of technical 
institutions before joining them.

Reforms in existing education system 
†654. PROF. M.M. AGARWAL: W ill the Minister of HUMAN 
RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government have formulated a national programme to bring 
reforms in the existing education system, for providing excellent training 
to teachers and to ensure uniformity in the fields of education: 
(b) If so, the details thereof; and 
(c) the details of the amount sanctioned to various States under the 
Centrally Sponsored Schemes during the last three years? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HUMAN RESOURCE 
DEVELOPMENT (SHRI M.A.A. FATMI): (a) to (c) The education system 
in the country is guided by the Na tional Policy on Education, 1986 (as 
modified in 1992) which, among other things, envisages that effective 
measures will be taken in the dire ction of the common school system. 
The Policy also envisages overhauling of the system of teacher education 
in the country with emphasis on continuing education and the need for 
teachers to meet the thrusts envisaged in the policy. 
Educational Reforms are a continuous process. A Committee of the 
Central Advisory Board of Education has been constituted on 8.9.2004 
under the Chairmanship of Shri Tarun Gogoi, Chief Minister of Assam on 
the subject of 'Girls Education and the common school system'. The 
National Council for Teacher Education, a statutory body, is responsible 
for regulation and the proper observance of norms and standards in teacher 
education at the Elementary and Secondary levels. The revised Teacher 
Education Scheme for the Tenth Plan period envisages establishment of 
one District Institute of Education and Training (DIETV District Resource 
Centre (DRC) in every District and making them optimally functional and 
operational or improving the quality of programmes undertaken by them 
especially those of pre-service and in -service training so as to enable 
them to effectively play their nodal role in improving quality of Education, 
as measured in terms of levels of learner achievement. 
Three statements indicating the amounts released to various States/ 
UTs under Centrally Sponsored Schemes (Plan) during the years 
2001-02,2002-03 and 2003-04 are given in the Statement—I, II, III.

RAJYA SABHA [9 March, 2005] 
Illiteracy 
†655. PROF. MM. AGARWAL: Will the Minister of HUMAN 
RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that as on date more than 36 crore persons are 
illiterate in the country; 
(b) whether Government have formulated any time-bound programme in 
this regard; 
(c) if so, the details thereof; and 
(d) the effective steps being taken by Government to increase the literacy 
rate as well as to educate the illiterate people? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HUMAN RESOURCE 
DEVELOPMENT (SHRI M.A.A. FATMI): (a) As per Census 2001, there 
were 30.41 crore non-literates in 7+age-group in the country. 
(b) to (d) In the Elementary Education Sector, Sarva Shiksha Abhiyan 
(SSA) has been launched with a holis tic and convergent approach, to 
implement Universalisation of Elementary Education in a mission mode 
with district focus. The goals of SSA are: 
• All children in School, Education Guarantee Centre, Alternate School, 
'Back-to-School' camp by 2003. 
• All children complete five years of primary schooling by 2007. 
• All children complete eight years of elementary schooling by 2010. 
• Focus on elementary education of satisfactory quality with emphasis 
on education for life. 
• Bridge all gender and social category gaps at primary stage by 
2007 and at elementary education level by 2010. 
• Universal retention by 2010. 
The National Literacy Mission (NLM) aims to provide functional literacy 
to non-literates in 15-35 age group. The target of NLM is to attain a 
sustainable threshold literacy rate of  75% of 2007. The thrust areas of 
NLM are improving female literacy in low female literacy areas, to organize 
residual illiteracy projects in areas,  which have substantial number of 
illiterates, and to set up continuing education centre s for providing 
opportunities for life long learning to the neo-literates.

Fee Structure for IIM 
660. SHRI KALRAJ MISHRA. Will the Minister of HUMAN RESOURCE 
DEVELOPMENT be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government have thrashed out the question of fee structure 
for the Indian Institutes of Management, and the autonomy to be enjoyed 
by these Institutes and their managements; and 
(b) if so, the outcome thereof, indicating the policy laid down as a result 
thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HUMAN RESOURCE 
DEVELOPMENT (SHRI M.A.A. FATMI): (a) Yes, Sir. Indian Institutes of 
Management continue to enjoy functional autonomy. 
(b) The broad policy for the fee st ructure of Indian Institutes of 
Management is as follows: 
(i) All the IIMs will provide a need-based scholarship to both the first 
and second year students; 
(ii) All the students admitted, whose annual gross family income is 
Rs. 2.00 lakh and below, will be eligible for scholarships up to a 
full tuition fee waiver. 
The IIMs are empowered to take all decisions regarding fee structure.

RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that a large number of students are not able to 
pursue their education upto middle or secondary stages because of lack

(b) if so, the percentage of such dropouts;

(d) Some of the steps taken by the Government to reduce the dropout 
rate are:

years. 
— Monitoring of attendance by the community. 
— Micro planning and household survey to identify the dropouts and 
reasons therefor. 
— Organising retention drives. 
— Improving the quality of teaching to retain children in school. 
— Organising bridge courses/back to  school camps etc. to bring 
the dropouts back into school.

"universalisation of primary education" by increasing enrolment, 
retention and attendance and simultaneously impacting on the

Leakage of results of CAT Examinations 
As per the report received from the Indian Institute of Management, 
Ahmedabad (IIMA), CAT 2004 was conducted on November 21, 2004. 
Answer sheets were scanned by each of the institutes immediately after 
that. On December 1, the admissi on chairmen of all the IIMs and the 
Common Admission Test (CAT) center coordinators met at CAT Center to 
do all necessary checks for processing  of the results. The final CDs 
containing the scores and the confirmed complete addresses were sent 
to all the IIMs and to the scorecard-printing agency on December 15, 
2004. 
The CAT group decided internally that by midnight December 21/22, 
2004, the results would be displayed on the websites of all IIMs and that 
posting of the scorecards would also start simultaneously. This was an 
internal decision, and there was no public announcement about this date. 
Before displaying the scorecards on their respective websites, each

institute goes through a process of te sting from the view point of easy 
accessibility prior to uploading on to the website. The testing for the IIMA

uploading and testing on-line, it is possible that some candidates may 
have got access to the link by mere coincidence. As the whole operation 
is to be in the public domain in any case, such coincidences would be 
inconsequential in terms of the ultimate outcome. Moreover, only the 
individuals who furnish the respective Test Registration Number and Date

the objective of providing better service to the test takers. The exercise of 
prior testing was meant to ensure a smooth and trouble free access to 
everyone.

the website of each IIM by midnight of December 21/22, 2004.

(a) the reasons for increase in child prostitution; 
(b) whether Government have taken or propose to take any effective 
measures to prevent this evil; 
(c) if so, the details thereof; and 
(d) the cases of child prostitution that have been reported during last 
three years, State-wise and the action taken so far by Government? 
THE MINISTER OF HUMAN R ESOURCE DEVELOPMENT (SHRI 
ARJUN SINGH): (a) The reasons attributed to child prostitution are poverty, 
illiteracy, unemployment, increasing tourism, industrialization, demand 
of children for commercial sex and breaking up of traditional family system. 
(b) and (c) Yes, Sir. In addition to the existing overall constitutional and 
legal framework like IPC and ITRA which prohibit exploitation of women 
and children for commercial sexual exploitation, the Government has 
prepared a National Plan of Action for Combating Trafficking of Women 
and Children 1998 which, inter alia, envisages Prevention, Awareness 
Generation and Social Mobilisation, Health Care Services, Education and 
Child Care, Housing, Shelter and Civic Amenities, Economic Empowerment, 
Legal Reforms & Law Enforcement, Rescue and Rehabilitation, Institutional 
Machinery and Methodology. The State Governments have been directed 
to take appropriate measures to implement National Plan of Action. Immoral 
Traffic (Prevention) Act 1956 is being made more stringent for traffickers, 
brothel keepers, pimps, clients to curb the demand and supply. The other 
activities include awareness campaign through TV. and Radio, sensitization 
of police and lower judiciary and involvement of NGOs in prevention and 
rescue activities. 
(d) The incidence reported with regard to procuration of minor girls, 
buying and selling of girls for prostitution and importation of girls during 
last three years as provided by National Crime Record Bureau is given in 
the Statement (See below). Since law and order is a state subject, the 
State Government take necessary ac tion is such cases. The Central 
Government provides financial support to NGOs and Government 
Organisations for prevention, rescue and rehabilitation of child victims.

690. SHRI DATTAMEGHE: Will the Minister of HUMAN RESOURCE 
DEVELOPMENT be pleased to state: 
(a) whether a Centrally-Sponsor ed Scheme, the Kasturba Gandhi 
Balika Vidyalaya (KGBV) scheme was prepared in the Tenth Five Year 
Plan; 
(b) the salient features thereof; 
(c) whether under this scheme, Government have set up some residential 
schools in tribal areas for girls from backward communities; 
(d) if so, the details thereof; and 
(e) the names of States where schools under this KGBV Scheme are 
to be set up and the amount so far released to each State to set up these 
schools? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN  THE MINISTRY OF HUMAN 
RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT (SHRI M.A. A. FATMI): (a) to (e) The 
Government of India has launched a new scheme called Kasturba Gandhi 
Balika Vidyalaya (KGBV) for setting up upto 750 residential schools 
with boarding facilities at el ementary level for girls belonging 
predominantly to the SC, ST, OBC and minority communities in 
Educationally Backward Blocks (EBBs) where the female rural literacy 
is below the national average and the gender gap in literacy is more 
than the national average. In particular, areas with concentration of 
tribal population, SC, OBC and minority populations, or areas with a 
large number of small, scattered habitations that do not otherwise qualify 
for an elementary school will be covered. 
In view of the targeted nature of  the scheme, minimum 75% of the 
enrolment in these residential school s shall be reserved for girls from 
SC, ST, OBC or minority communities and for the remaining 2 57o, 
priority would be accorded to girls from families below the poverty line. 
A provision of Rs. 489 crore has been made for the Scheme during 
10th Plan period. The financing pattern of the scheme will be in the ratio 
of 75:25 between the Centre and the States during the Tenth Five Year 
Plan. 
The number of KGBV schools and funds sanctioned State-wise is given 
in the statement.

Preparation of annual report by Prasar Bharati 
693. SHRI K. RAMA MOHANA RAO: Will the Minister of INFORMATION 
AND BROADCATING be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that even after seven years of its existence, 
Prasar Bharati has not prepared even a single Annual Report; 
(b) whether it is also a fact that preparation of Annual Report is mandatory 
under the Prasar Bharati Act; and 
(c) if so, the reasons for not preparing the Annual Reports? 
THE MINISTER OF INFORMATION AND BROADCATING (SHRI S. 
JAIPAL REDDY): (a) to (c) Section 32(2)(k) of Prasar Bharati Act stipulates 
that the Central Government may by notification, make rules, which may 
provide the form in which and the time within which, the Corporation shall 
prepare their Annual Report under Section 31 of the said Act. The 
Government on 18th May, 2004, notified the rules in this regard, which are 
known as Prasar Bharati (Broadcasting Corporation of India), Annual Report 
of the Corporation Rules, 2004. Prasar Bharati has set in motion the process 
of preparation of Annual Report as required under the Prasar Bharati. Act. 
Prior to issuance of these rules, the information pertaining to the Prasar 
Bharati has been incorporated in the Annual Report of the Ministry of 
Information & Broadcasting.

694. SHRI VIJAY J. DARDA: Will the Minister of INFORMATION AND 
BROADCASTING be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government are aware that Geetakrishnan Committee on 
Expenditure Reforms had recommended that DAVP should be wound up; 
(b) if so, what is Government's reaction thereto; 
(c) when the existing guidelines relating to advertisement policy were framed; 
(d) whether views of the newspaper industry were taken into consideration 
at that point of time; and 
(e) as these guidelines are required to be revised urgently in consultation 
with the newspaper industry by when Governement propose to do that? 
THE MINISTER OF INFORMATION AND BROADCASTING (SHRI S. 
JAIPAL REDDY): (a) The Geetakrishnan Committee on Expenditure 
312 

[9 March, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
Reforms had recommended that the ac tivities of the Directorate of 
Advertising & Visual Publicity (DAVP) including release of advertisements, 
could be decentralised and left to the individual Ministries/Departments 
and DAVP should concern itself with establishment of rate contracts relating 
to advertisements to be followed by various Ministries. 
(b) The Government is of the view that if the activities of DAVP are 
decentralised, the Ministries/Departments could need more staff than that 
with DAVP at present and thereby defeat the very purpose of economy in 
Government. DAVP has been providing facilities at single point with various 
inputs including plan, design, language versions, multi-media requirements 
and maintenance of fairness and balance among different categories of 
newspapers across the country. Moreover, DAVP is able to secure less 
than the market prices for Government by virtue of being bulk purchases of 
space in print media. The Government is, therefore, not inclined to amend 
the Allocation of Business Rules to allow the Ministries/Departments to 
advertise directly to newspapers. However, in order to rationalize DAVP 
structure and bring in economy, 114 posts in DAVP have now been identified 
for abolition, out of which, 37 posts have already been abolished. 
(c) to (e) The existing guidelines relating to the Advertisement Policy 
have come into force with effect from 1 st May, 2002. These guidelines are 
revised from time to time keeping in view the changing circumstances in 
consultation with newspaper associations.

Statement 
Monitoring of EPICs 
The Election Commission of India is directly responsible for the 
implementation and monitoring of the scheme of Elector's Photo Identity 
Cards (EPICs). An extract of information received from the Commission in 
the matter is given below:— 
"The Commission had received some complaints regarding persons 
possessing Electroral Photo Identity Cards (EPIC) who could not caste 
their vote during the General Elections to Lok Sabha and State Legislative 
Assemblies of Andhra Pradesh, Karnataka, Orissa and Sikkim conducted 
in April-May, 2004, as their names were missing from the electoral rolls 
used for the conduct of these elections. The Commission had forwarded 
all complaints received by it to the Chief Electoral Officers concerned for 
appropriate action to restore the ent ries and to ascertain the reasons 
behind the missing names. 
The general elections to the State Legislative Assemblies of Arunachal 
Pradesh and Maharashtra were due to be held in September-October, 
2004. No complaints were received during the general election to Lok 
Sabha in Arunachal Pradesh about omission of names of persons 
possessing Electroral Photo Identity Cards (EPIC). However, there were 
some such complaints received from the State of Maharashtra. Therefore,

Coparcenary rights of women 
714. SHRIMATI SUSHMA SWARAJ: W ill the Minister of LAW AND 
JUSTICE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government are aware of the Hindu Succession Andhra 
Pradesh (Amendment) Act, 1986 and the changes it has brought about in 
the rights of daughters in relation to ancestral property of Hindus; 
(b). whether the national Commission for Women has carried out a study 
of the coparcenary rights of women in Andhra Pradesh in the light of this 
amendment; and 
332 

[9 March, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
(c) the recommendations made in the report and the action taken 
thereon? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF LAW AND JUSTICE 
(SHRI K. VENKATAPATHY): (a) Yes, Sir. 
(b) and (c) A study sponsored by the National Commission for Women 
on coparcenary rights of women in Andhra Pradesh was conducted by 
NALSAR, University of Law, Hyderabad. The project report submitted by 
NALSAR to the National Commission for Women, inter alia, contains the 
following suggestions:— 
"(i) The coparcenary should be done away with in Hindu Succession 
Act, 1956 as we have in 1956 done away with Stridhana. 
(ii) Equal share to daughter along with son in the ancestral property 
should be done on the lines of Section 8 of the Hindu succession 
Act, 1956, which confers equal share in self-acquired property. 
(iii) The right to claim partition should be given to daughter along with 
sons and predeceased son's wife/widow. 
(iv) The members of Joint Hindu Family can still continue and those 
of them who wish to stay toget her can stay as co-owners of 
property." 
The Law Commission of India, a fter studying the various State 
amendments to the Hindu Succession Act, 1956 including the Hindu 
Succession (Andhra Pradesh Amendment) Act, 1986 and the Kerala Joint 
Hindu Family System (Abolition) Act, 1975 submitted its 174th Report on 
"Property Rights of Women : Proposed Reforms under the Hindu Law" to 
the Central Government. With a view to implementing the said Report of 
the Commission and after consulting the State Governments, the Hindu 
Succession (Amendment) Bill, 2004 was introduced in the Rajya Sabha 
on the 20th December, 2004. The Bill is currently under examination of the 
Department Related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Personnel, 
Public Grievances, Law and Justice.

717. SHRI B.K. HARIPRASAD: Will the Minister of LAW AND JUSTICE

accommodation for judicial officials at the level of district courts to insulate 
them from various unethical influences caused by lack of Government 
support;

and the details of its findings thereon; and

to unethical tendencies? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF LAW AND JUSTICE 
(SHRI K. VENKATAPATHY): (a) to (c) No, Sir. There is no proposal with 
the Central Government to provide official accommodation for judicial officials 
at the level of district courts to insulate them from various unethical 
influences caused by lack of Government support. The Supreme Court, in

Governments are responsible for providing requisite facilities to the judicial 
officers of their States.

Planning Commission, provides funds to the State Governments and Union 
Territories for construction of residential accommodation for the judicial 
officers, under the Centrally Sponsored Scheme. The State Governments

Under utilization of funds allocated for disabled persons 
732. DR. NARAYAN SINGH MANAKLAO: Will the Minister of SOCIAL 
JUSTICE AND EMPOWERMENT be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that near ly Rs. 198 crores remained unspent 
from the budgetary outlay for the disabled in the Ninth Five Year Plan 
under Central schemes; 
(b) if so, the reasons therefor; 
(c) whether any steps have been taken to utilise allocated resources for 
the disabled in the Tenth Five Year Plan; 
(d) if so, the details thereof; 
(e) the role of the Chief Commissioner for persons with disabilities in 
implementation of the schemes and over seeing of expenditure; and 
(f) whether Government plan for any radical change in the existing set 
up? 
THE MINISTER OF SOCIAL JUSTICE AND EMPOWERMENT 
(SHRIMATI MEIRA KUMAR): (a) and (b) The utilization of funds is measured 
as difference in Revised Estimates and actual expenditure. Thus, the 
unspent amount for disability sector for the IX Plan was Rs.35.07 crores 
and not Rs.198 crores as reported. Major reasons for non-utilisation of 
funds were: 
(a) State Governments took time to formulate projects and set up 
mechanism for implementation. 
(b) The office of CCD could be set up only by the middle of the XI Plan 
due to administrative procedure involved in getting required clearances/ 
approval. 
(c) and (d) Yes, Sir. During the 10t h Five Year Plan, an amount of 
Rs. 194.05 crore and Rs.168.92 crores had been utilized out of an revised 
budget estimate of Rs192.37 crores and Rs. 186.25 crores allocated for 
the year 2002-03 and 2003-04, respectively. Full utilization of allocated 
funds depends on various factor viz. the timely submission of inspection 
reports, recommendations of the State Govemments/UT Administrations, 
receipt of utilization certificates from the non-governmental organizations 
receiving grants etc. 
(e) The Chief Commissioner for Persons with Disabilities (CCD) is a 
statutory authority having powers under the Persons with Disabilities Act, 
354 

[9 March, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
1995. The functions and duties of the Chief Commissioner include inter-
a//a, monitoring utilization of funds disbursed by the Central Government. 
(f) No, Sir.

737. SHRI C. PERUMAL: Will the Minister of SOCIAL JUSTICE AND

and educational institution for disabled;

reservation policy? 
THE MINISTER OF SOCIAL JUSTICE AND EMPOWERMENT 
(SHRIMATI MEIRA KUMAR): (a) and (b) Yes Sir. Section 33 of the Persons 
with Disabilities Act, 1995 provides that every appropriate Government 
shall provide for reservation of not less than 3% of vacancies in identified 
posts in every establishment for perso ns with disabilities of which one

low vision; (ii) hearing impairment and (iii) locomotor disability or cerebral

institutions and other educational in stitutions receiving aid from the 
Government, shall reserve not less than three per cent seats for persons 
with disabilities.

765. SHRI RAJKUMAR DHOOT: W ill the Minister of URBAN 
EMPLOYMENT AND POVERTY ALLEVIATION be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that UNICEF report "State of the World's Children-

EMPLOYMENT AND POVERTY ALLEVIATION (KUMARI SELJA) 
(a) No, Sir. 
(b) to (d) As per the estimate by the Town & Country Planning 
Organisation (TCPO) for the year 2001, the urban slum population is 
618.258 lakh. Slums consist of kuchcha/temporary houses in which children 
are living along with other family members. As per the Census 2001, the 
number of urban households in temporary houses is 3,48,15,619. In order 
to facilitate construction and upgradation of dwelling units for the urban 
slum dwellers below the poverty line and to provide health and enabling 
urban environment through community  toilets, the Ministry of Urban 
Employment & Poverty alleviation is implementing a Centrally Sponsored 
scheme called Valmiki Ambedkar Awas Yojana (VAMBAY). No time frame 
has been fixed to free the urban areas from kuchcha houses.

DR. P.C. ALEXANDER (Maharashtra): Mr. Vice-Chairman, Sir, I rise 
to move the two amendments for which I had given notice and I wish to focus 
only on the two problems which I have mentioned in my notice. The first is the 
failure on the part of the President's Address to make mention about the need 
and importance of comprehensive statutor y reforms to improve the working of 
political parties in our country and the second is the failure to mention the 
need for a total restructuring of the educ ational system to serve certain wider 
objectives mentioned in the Preamble of  the Constitution, particularly for 
promoting national integration and unity. 
If we look at the last 58 years of our Independence and our 
experiments in the working of  the parliamentary system of democracy, we will 
have to admit honestly that we had not come up to the expectations which 
were made in the framing of the Constitution by the founding fathers of our 
Republic. Actually, if we make an assessment on the performance of our 
country for 58 years of the working of  the parliamentary system, we will have 
to admit that we have not done well. But still we are persisting with that system 
hoping that we will improve as years go by. If you ask me honestly to give my 
assessment as to where we have failed in making a success of the system, I 
will have absolutely no hesitation in putting my finger on the poor working of 
the political parties in our country. In  my judgement, this is the number one 
reason why the parliamentary system has not succeeded to the extent it 
should have in our country. It is the basic condition of the parliamentary 
democracy that it is successful only if there is the pr emise of a sound 
parliamentary system. If we look at wh at we have achieved over the last 58 
years, we will say with great regret that we have not succeeded in evolving 
healthy national parties. In a huge sub- continent like ours with over a billion 
people, we still have Governments run by national parties but with the help of 
a large multiplicity of small parties. If we look at the State Governments also, 
we will find that the State parties them selves do not have the real strength to 
run the Government and they 
461 

RAJYA SABHA [9 March, 2005]  
are in turn dependent on small parties. I consider it a very serious threat to the 
future of parliamentary democracy in our country. Sir, if we look back when the 
Congress Party contested elections after three years of Independence, i.e. in 
1952, there were 74 small parties contesting the elections along with the 
Congress Party. But the Congress Party won 364 seats out of 489 seats. By 
1957, the number of parties was betw een 80 and 90 and the Congress Party 
won 371 seats out of 493. In  1952, the second largest party in Parliament next 
to the Congress Party which had 364 seats, had only 12 Members. In 1957, 
the second largest party had only 19 Members. Just think of the situation 
today. After the 1999 elections, the two major national parties, i.e. the 
Congress Party and the BJP have really performed miserably, if I may use this 
word. The party which is running the Government today or leading the coalition 
today, has just 145 Members on its own and the single largest Opposition 
Party today has just 138 Members in a House of 540 Members. In a 
parliamentary democracy, the ruling party whether it leads the coalition or runs 
the Government, should be somewhere near the half way mark and if it does 
not depend on others, it should certainl y have more than the half way mark. 
The opposition party which is claiming to run the Government by defeating the 
party in power, should be near that mark. 
But these two great national parties have declined and they are on 
the road to decline for various reasons which I want to mention before you. Sir, 
I have 10 minutes only according to the time that you have allotted me... 
THE VICE-CHAIRMAN (SHRI SANTOSH BAGRODIA): Twelve 
minutes. 
DR. P.C. ALEXANDER: Therefore, I will rush through them. I, in my 
analysis, have identified seven major reasons as to why the national parties, 
including the Congress (I) and the BJP, have declined over the last 10 years. 
    
The first reason, in my opinion, is absence of inner party democracy. I 
am sorry to use this word; nomination cu lture has become the rule of political 
parties in our country. The only excepti on I would say is the Communist Party; 
I am not a great admirer of the Communist Party (Marxist), but all credit to 
them because I read with great interest from newspapers about Kerala where 
elections were held at the district level;  then elections were held at the State 
level, and then the State Party's 
462 

[9 March, 2005] RAJYA SABHA  
Secretariat emerged as a result of elec tions at all the levels necessary. But 
what we see with other political parties , not only the big political parties, the 
national parties, but also other State parties,  is that it is all nomination culture 
there. They meet at the headquarters whether in Delhi or Lucknow or Patna, 
wherever these may be, and a few pe ople sit together and decide who should 
be the members of the Working Commi ttee, who should be the CPCC 
President or the State Party President and who should be the nominee for 
elections to this post or that post. This is the negation of democracy. If we 
believe in democratic principles, we should practise it in our own party. But 
because we do not allow inner party democracy, we find the national parties 
today at the beck and call of small pa rties which have a strength of two or 
three or, as in Kerala, there is even a one-member party. 
The second major reason out of the seven which I have identified is, 
erosion of accountability in  these parties. We talk of accountability of the 
Government to Parliament. But where is the accountability of the leaders of 
the parties to their parties' organisat ions? When an MP or an MLA is elected, 
because he had been nominated to be a candidate from a particular 
constituency, not by the members of the party in that constituency but by the 
High Commands sitting in New Delhi, Patna or Lucknow, how can he be 
accountable to the members in the constituency? He is accountable to his 
High Command; otherwise he will not get nominated for the second time. It is 
a very dangerous practice that we ar e following. Mr. Deputy Chairman, this 
never happens in an advanced democracy. I am a very close student of the 
Parliamentary system in the United Kingdom, and I can say from my own 
personal observation that no Prime Minister, no party leader, will ever think of 
telling the Constituency, "So and so is going to be your candidate. You vote for 
him." The Constituency alone has the right to elect or select a person who is to 
be their candidate. 
The third reason is -- I am using a strong term -- the so-called High 
Commands of parties stifling leadership at the local levels. This is a new 
development. It never happened in Pandit Jawaharlal Nehru's long period of 
time. In Nehru's time, the High Command depended upon strong leaders at 
the State level. Today the leaders at th e State level cannot be qualified as 
strong, and they are totally dependent on their existence; they are at the beck 
and call of the people sitting in these Headquarters. Think of the days when 
Shri Kamaraj was the Chief Minister of Tamil Nadu from 1954 to 1965 -- 11 
long years and nobody disturbed him.   Dr. B.C. Roy was 
463 

RAJYA SABHA [9 March, 2005]  
the Chief Minister of Bengal from 1948 to 1962. Govind Vallabh Pant remained 
Chief Minister from 1946 to 1965. Shri Pratap Singh Kairon remained Chief 
Minister from 1956-64. These were th e tall stalwarts who strengthened the 
national parties. The national party leaders derived strength from these 
stalwarts unlike today where the local leaders are waiting for the orders and 
diktats from the Headquarters. 
My fourth reason is 'consciously allowing groupism in party 
organisations in States'. I say 'consciously' because -- I am sorry again to 
make a very strong statement -- people who control the party at the top do not 
like strong partymen at the State level. So, they allow groups to fight against 
each other; they cancel their strength; and all groups depend upon the Centre. 
The fifth point is about defections from one party to another. An 
honest attempt is being made to prevent defections. But we are seeing 
devious ways in which people in Goa ar e trying to get round their act against 
this. Instead of jumping from one party to the other, they are resigning from 
their seats. Future historians will refer to chapters like this and this would 
create derision and contempt of our generation who tried to get round the rules 
and tried to invent devices by which yo u can defeat democracy while talking in 
defence of democracy. 
The sixth reason for the decline of democracy is the absence of any 
training course, absence even of any orientation course. Why is it so, Mr. Vice-
Chairman? Leaders arrive at the top. They themselves would never have 
fought an election. Most of them come to Rajya Sabha. Some of them come to 
Rajya Sabha without ever having won an election as an MLA, leave alone the 
Lok Sabha election. And the result is, you find inexperienced people running 
party organisations. And when they are inexperienced, they should have, at 
least, the humility to pick up the robes by undergoing training courses and 
orientation courses. Even in advanced c ountries, there are training courses. 
But we do not have them. The Parliament, of course, conducts such training 
courses; the Secretariats conduct them. But, at the party level, training courses 
are particularly neglected. 
The seventh reason, of course, is the low level of political morality. 
We are willing to change parties, labels, as we change our clothes.   The 
shameful record of defections in our country will go down in the history as 
464 

[9 March, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
one of the shameful records in any democratic country anywhere in the world.   
I recall the statistics of defections...
